content: In the context of nursing management, certain roles involve responsibilities such as budgetary control, staff rostering, approving pay claims, purchasing equipment, and assigning tasks. In smaller wards or shared responsibility settings, one nurse often assumes the role of the senior ward manager. Historically, these nurses were graded as G or H, but under the current system, they are classified within bands 6 to 8c. Above the ward level, there are positions such as Clinical Nurse Managers. These individuals oversee entire departments or multiple wards. Their involvement in clinical nursing or management varies depending on the preferences of the trust and the individual. Previously employed at H grade, they are now typically classified under band 7, with occasional placements in bands 8a or 8b under the Agenda for Change system. Modern Matrons were introduced to address perceived deficiencies in nursing skills and competence. They are responsible for overseeing all nursing activities within a department or directorate. Historically employed at H or I grades, they are now most commonly placed in bands 8a, 8b, or 8c, with occasional placements in band 7. For more details on this role and its historical roots, refer to the Matron section. The hierarchy of specialist nurses varies, as each specialist nurse has a distinct role within their respective NHS organization. However, they are generally experienced nurses and are employed at least at band 6, which corresponds to the former F grade. Pay Scales Until recently, all NHS nurses were employed under a system known as clinical grading. This system, also referred to as the Whitley system, categorized nurses and some other hospital staff into grades ranging from A (most junior) to I (most senior). Unregistered staff were employed on grades A and B (and occasionally C), while second-level nurses were employed on grades C to E. First-level nurses occupied grades D to I. This system remains popular among nurses, who often refer to themselves by their old clinical grade rather than their Agenda for Change band. Agenda for Change The Agenda for Change system was developed by the NHS to address criticisms of the clinical grading system, which was perceived to prioritize length of service over knowledge, responsibility, and skills. This system categorizes nurses and most other non-medical/dental staff into bands ranging from 2 to 9. Unregistered staff occupy bands 2 to 4, while qualified staff are placed in bands 5 to 8. Band 9 is reserved for the most senior NHS management positions, with no current nursing roles in this band. The principle of this system is equal pay for work of equal value, aiming to resolve discrepancies between grade and actual work performed under the clinical grading system. As of spring 2006, the pay scales for each band are as follows: Band 2: £12,177 £15,107 Band 3: £14,037 £16,799 Band 4: £16,405 £19,730 Band 5: £19,166 £24,803 Band 6: £22,886 £31,004 Band 7: £27,622 £36,416 Band 8a: £35,232 £42,278 Band 8b: £41,038 £50,733 Band 8c: £49,381 £60,880 Band 8d: £59,189 £73,281 Most nurses in England and Wales are now employed under Agenda for Change terms. However, some remain on clinical grades, particularly in Scotland, where only 9% of the workforce has transitioned. Despite government targets for full transition, a complete shift to the new system has not yet been achieved.
